title: SDP and offer/answer
summary: How to read an SDP body, and how RFC 3264 matches offers to answers without reordering streams.

lessons.title: The lines in an SDP body
lessons.summary: Read v, o, s, c, t, m, and a lines as a session description. RFC 8866 is the current SDP specification.
objectives: Name the session lines and the media lines
State that RFC 8866 obsoletes RFC 4566 and where status is decided
Separate the connection address from the RTP packets

illustration.title: One SDP body, top to bottom
illustration.caption: Session lines apply until an m-line starts a stream. Media lines and their a-lines belong to that stream.

paragraphs: RFC 8866 is the current SDP specification, and it obsoletes RFC 4566. The RFC Editor status banner on each document is the authority for that status, so a page that still quotes only 4566 is checked against the banner before it is treated as current.

The addresses 203.0.113.10, 203.0.113.20, 198.51.100.30, and 192.0.2.40 are documentation addresses from RFC 5737, and the telephone number in these labs is +15551212 at example.com. They exist so a trace can be shared without pointing at a real network.

A body starts with v=0, an o= origin that carries a session id and a session version, an s= name, a c= connection address, and a t= time. The c= line names where media should be sent, and it is an address inside the description, not a sample of audio.

Each m= line opens one media stream and lists a port, a transport, and payload types. a= lines after that m= line belong to that stream, while a session-level a= line is only the default for streams that do not override it.

lessons.title: Same m-lines, same order
lessons.summary: RFC 3264 matches streams by position. The answer has the same number of m-lines, in the same order.
objectives: Count m-lines in the offer and in the answer
Reject a stream without deleting its position
Keep later offers in the same order

illustration.title: Position is the match
illustration.caption: Stream 1 stays stream 1. A rejected second stream is still the second m-line.

paragraphs: The answer must contain the same number of m-lines as the offer, and those lines stay in the same order. RFC 3264 uses that position to decide which answer stream belongs to which offered stream, so dropping a line or swapping two lines breaks the match.

The media type and the transport on an accepted line must match the offer. A second audio line in the offer is still a second audio line in the answer, even when the answerer only wants the first codec.

To refuse one stream, the answer sets that m-line port to 0 and still includes a media type, a protocol, and a format list. The refused stream occupies the same slot, which is why the following lines do not slide up.
A later offer in the same dialog keeps those positions. RFC 6337 is the usage document that shows how easy it is to break a call by rebuilding the m-line list from scratch.

lessons.title: rtpmap names and fmtp parameters
lessons.summary: Match codecs by the rtpmap encoding name. The G.722 rtpmap clock stays 8000.
objectives: Match dynamic codecs by encoding name
Recite the static payload types 0, 8, 9, and 18
Keep the G.722 rtpmap clock at 8000

illustration.title: Names that survive a payload-type change
illustration.caption: Static types may omit rtpmap. Dynamic types are meaningless until rtpmap names them. G722/8000 is the required clock.

paragraphs: A dynamic payload type is a number from 96 through 127, and that number has no codec meaning until a=rtpmap assigns an encoding name. RFC 3264 matching uses the encoding name, so payload type 96 for opus and payload type 111 for opus are the same codec.

Static payload types from RFC 3551 include 0 PCMU/8000, 8 PCMA/8000, 9 G722/8000, and 18 G729/8000, and those names apply even when rtpmap is omitted. Writing the rtpmap anyway is legal, and it is how you show the clock you expect the peer to use.

sections.h: fmtp belongs to one payload type
paragraphs: a=fmtp parameters apply only to the payload type named on that line, on that m-line. Accept a format parameter only when you implement it, and reject that payload type instead of guessing when the parameter is unknown.

The G.722 line is the clock-rate trap inside an otherwise ordinary rtpmap attribute, and the token you write is G722/8000 even though the audio sample rate is 16 kHz, because RFC 3551 fixed the RTP clock at 8000. A 20 ms packet advances the timestamp by 160 on that 8000 Hz clock, and rewriting the clock to 16000 will miss a peer that followed the RFC.

lessons.title: Direction attributes and hold
lessons.summary: sendrecv, sendonly, recvonly, and inactive are per stream. Hold is commonly sendonly or inactive.
objectives: List the four direction attributes
Answer sendonly with recvonly or inactive
Place a call on hold without c=0.0.0.0

illustration.title: Legal answers
illustration.caption: The answer direction is from the answerer. Hold offers are commonly sendonly or inactive.

sections.h: Direction is a property of the stream
paragraphs: Each stream is sendrecv, sendonly, recvonly, or inactive, and a media-level attribute overrides a session-level default. The answer uses the answerer's point of view, so an offer of sendonly is answered with recvonly or with inactive.

sendrecv means the agent will send and receive, sendonly means it will send and does not want to receive, and recvonly means it will only receive media on that stream. inactive means the agent will do neither, and an inactive offer is answered with inactive.

Hold is commonly sendonly, when the holder still sends such as music, or inactive, when neither side should send. The peer answers sendonly with recvonly, or answers inactive with inactive, in a new offer/answer exchange such as a re-INVITE.
Do not put a call on hold by setting c=IN IP4 0.0.0.0. RFC 3264 retired that old behavior because it breaks RTCP and IPv6, and RFC 6337 is the usage document for this family of mistakes.

objectives: Write a rejection as port 0

illustration.title: Refuse without renumbering
illustration.caption: The second stream is unused. It is still the second m-line.

paragraphs: Set the answer port to 0 to reject that offered stream. RFC 3264 still requires the media type, the transport protocol, and a format list on that line, so m=audio 0 RTP/AVP 0 is a refusal and not a blank line.
Use port 0 when the answerer has no payload type in common with that m-line. Omitting the m-line is a different bug, the count bug, and it mis-numbers every later stream.

A re-offer that wants the stream to stay rejected offers it again at port 0 in the same position, and the answer also uses port 0 there. Adding a new stream means appending a new m-line, not recycling a rejected slot's place in line.
An offered port of 0 must be rejected. Do not answer a zero offer port with a real port, and do not treat port 0 as a request to pick a port of your own.

lessons.title: Early media and 183
lessons.summary: 183 Session Progress with SDP is the usual early-media pattern. 180 means ringing. A 183 does not always have SDP.
objectives: Recognize 183 with SDP as a usual early-media pattern
Treat 180 as ringing
Read a 183 that has no SDP as still a 183

illustration.title: Progress is not one body
illustration.caption: This ladder's 183 happens to carry SDP. 180 is ringing and has no SDP here. A 183 is allowed to omit SDP.

sections.h: 183 is progress, and SDP is optional on it
paragraphs: RFC 3960 describes early media, and the usual pattern is 183 Session Progress carrying SDP so the caller can play an announcement or remote ringback. A 183 does not always contain SDP, so you read the body of that message instead of treating the status code as proof of media.

180 Ringing means the far end is alerting, and when that 180 has no SDP the caller generates local ringback unless early media from an earlier 183 is already playing. Keep those two jobs separate, because ringing is not the same event as early media.

A provisional response is not reliable unless RFC 3262 applies, which means Require 100rel, an RSeq, and a PRACK. If the INVITE carried the offer, a reliable 183 can carry the answer, and an unreliable 183 with SDP is a common carrier pattern that is not the same thing as a finished reliable answer.
Read the SDP in the 200 OK to the INVITE as well. Early-media ports and the final answer ports can differ, and RFC 6337 is the usage document when those two bodies disagree.

lessons.title: Offer/answer pitfalls in RFC 6337
lessons.summary: RFC 6337 is the usage document for offer/answer mistakes: order, version, delayed offer, and hold.
objectives: Increment the SDP session version when the description changes
Tell an early offer from a delayed offer
Stop using a zero connection address as hold

illustration.title: Four ways an answer goes wrong
illustration.caption: RFC 3264 is the rule. RFC 6337 is where the same mistakes show up in real exchanges.

layers.name: Order
layers.detail: Lines swapped or a slot reused

paragraphs: RFC 6337 is the offer/answer usage document that operators open when a locally reasonable SDP still fails. It does not replace RFC 3264, and it shows the failures that follow from rebuilding SDP instead of editing it, including dropped m-lines, swapped m-lines, and payload types matched by number.

When the SDP you send is different from the SDP you sent before, increment the sess-version in o=. Peers treat an unchanged version as the same description, so a hold or a new port hidden under the old version is easy to ignore.

If the INVITE contains SDP, that body is the offer and the answer belongs in a reliable response. If the INVITE contains no SDP, the offer is in a reliable response from the far side and the answer is in the ACK, which is the delayed-offer pattern.

Do not put an answer in the 200 OK when the INVITE already carried the offer, and do not put a second offer in that 200 OK just because a 183 already answered. Read RFC 6337 when a call has SDP in more than one response.

The usage mistakes that operators repeat are hold via c=IN IP4 0.0.0.0, and deletion of a rejected m-line. Direction attributes perform hold, and port 0 performs rejection, and both leave the rest of the body aligned.
A codec change uses the rtpmap name, including G722/8000 rather than a rewritten 16000 Hz clock. RFC 6337 is the checklist you open after the rules in RFC 3264 are already in front of you.

quiz.q: RFC 6337 is best used as
choices: The usage document for offer/answer pitfalls
quiz.why: The rules stay in RFC 3264. RFC 6337 shows how they fail in practice.

quiz.q: When a new SDP differs from the previous one, you
choices: Keep the same sess-version so it looks stable
quiz.why: An unchanged session version tells the peer the description did not change.

quiz.q: An INVITE with no SDP means
choices: The offer will arrive in a reliable response, and the answer goes in the ACK
quiz.why: That is delayed offer. Early offer is SDP in the INVITE.

quiz.q: Matching payload type 96 to payload type 96 without rtpmap
choices: Is the pitfall. Match the encoding name
quiz.why: Dynamic numbers are not globally assigned.

quiz.q: Hold in a current offer uses
quiz.why: The zero connection address is the old hold behavior RFC 3264 moved away from.

quiz.q: Deleting a rejected m-line
quiz.why: Keep the line and set the port to 0.

fault.title: Session version left unchanged on hold
fault.symptom: A re-INVITE changes a=sendrecv to a=sendonly but o= still says session version 2890844526. The peer keeps sending media.
fault.log:
o=alice 2890844526 2890844526 IN IP4 203.0.113.10
previous direction a=sendrecv
new body direction a=sendonly
sess-version unchanged
choices: The session version did not increase, so the peer can treat the SDP as unchanged
fault.why: RFC 8866 uses sess-version to signal a modified session description.
fault.cause: The hold offer reused the previous version number, so the change looked like a retransmission of the old SDP.
fault.fix: Increment sess-version, keep a=sendonly or a=inactive, and do not signal hold with c=0.0.0.0.
